 Phil Tenser Digital Media Manager Tim Nazzaro Digital Content Editor Imani Clement Digital Content Editor BOSTON — Some Massachusetts voters encountered long lines at the polls Tuesday as they decided on nine statewide ballot questions and key races, including governor and U.S. Senate. It's part of the midterm election that could shape the balance of power in Congress and the direction for the country during the second half of President Donald Trump's term. Follow our live updates throughout Election Day and scroll down for a guide to everything you need to know about voting in the Bay State.

 Long lines
 Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin said that high turnout and the lengthy ballots are contributing to some reports of "longer wait times" at polling places. 
 "While these longer wait times are not widespread, I ask that voters be patient if there is a line to cast their ballot," Galvin said in a statement. "Local election officials are making every effort to expedite voters through the process. I also want to remind anyone who is voting later this evening that they will be allowed to vote as long as they are in line at their polling place at 8 p.m."
 Where to vote
 Polling places are open Tuesday from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Some could open as early as 5:45 a.m.
 To find your polling place, enter your street address into THIS TOOL from the Secretary of the Commonwealth's office.
 Who can vote
 There is no same-day registration for voters in Massachusetts, although one of the questions on the ballot could change that. 
 Voters are required to register 10 days before an election. In this case, the deadline was 11:59 p.m. on Oct. 24. 
 Those who requested a mail-in ballot can still vote in person if: 
 You applied to vote by mail, but never returned your ballot
 You mailed your ballot back, but it hasn’t reached your local election office
 Your ballot was received by your local election office, but it was rejected
 Polls close at 8 p.m., but anyone already in line before the deadline will be allowed to vote. Tabulation of ballots begins only after polls close.
 Voting by mail in Massachusetts? Here's how to track your ballot What's on the ballot
 Nine statewide ballot questions 
 U.S. Senator
 U.S. Representative
 Governor and Lieutenant Governor
 Attorney General
 Secretary of State
 Treasurer
 Auditor
 Governor’s Councillor
 State Senator
 State Representative
 District Attorney
 Register of Probate
 County Commissioner (certain counties only)
 County Treasurer (certain counties only)
 Sheriff (Franklin County – to fill vacancy)
 Additional local offices (vary by community) 
 Voter registration
 The total number of voters in Massachusetts grew by more than 100,000 between the deadlines for the September primary and the general election, according to data provided by the Secretary of the Commonwealth's office.
 Voters are required to register 10 days before an election, although one of the questions on the ballot could change that. In this case, the deadline was 11:59 p.m. on Oct. 24.
 According to the latest count, 5.2 million people are registered to vote in the general election. Of those, 24.17% are registered Democrats, 7.82% are registered Republicans and 67.11% are unenrolled.
 This content is imported from infogram. You may be able to find the same content in another format, or you may be able to find more information, at their web site. National balance of power
 Democrats are hoping that voters give them control of at least one chamber of Congress in this midterm election, and several New England races could play a role in deciding that contest. Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Rhode Island are all voting for a U.S. Senator. 
 In order for the Democrats to take control of the U.S. Senate, they would need to win 17 seats. Control of the U.S. House is held by whichever party holds at least 218 seats.
